# Meta to reevaluate net-zero timeline on the back of record emissions

Company reported a 45 percent increase in carbon footprint due to AI demand

November 20, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Social networking firm Meta is reevaluating its 2030 net-zero timeline amid record carbon emission levels, according to its latest sustainability report .
In the report, the company revealed its net carbon footprint increased by 45 percent in the last year, hitting 11.9 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (mtCO2e). The company’s location-based emissions inventory was recorded at almost twice that amount, at 21.7 million mtCO2e.

– Getty Images

Rachel Peterson, Meta’s VP of data centers, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, wrote that the company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones.” That includes the 2030 net zero timeframe and its near-term intensity targets. They said demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than expected, while interconnection queues, permitting, and transmission buildout have lagged. Meta did not give a new date and said it will share the outcome later.
"The path forward is complex, and the route may continue to evolve, but the outcomes we are working toward remain unchanged: to establish a long-term pathway to net zero emissions, to restore more water than we consume, and to build infrastructure in a way that supports surrounding communities and grids," they said in a statement.
The numbers reflect growing emissions across all the major hyperscalers, with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft all reporting double-digit increases in their latest sustainability reports.
Google saw an 18 percent year-on-year increase, with Amazon reporting a 16 percent increase and Microsoft revealing that its emissions had grown by 25 percent. Of the hyperscalers, Meta is the only company to announce a reevaluation of its 2030 commitment, acknowledging the rise, which it attributes to the expansion of AI data centers.
Much of the emissions growth is tied to increasing reliance on natural gas to circumvent grid connection delays in the US. The report stated that Meta may deploy on-site gas where utilities cannot deliver power and plans to buy low-methane certificates to offset some of its emissions. The company left the RE100 climate initiative in July this year, saying it could no longer meet the technical criteria because of investments in new gas power. Last year, the company signed a deal with utility Entergy to fund the construction of ten natural gas plants to power its up to 5GW Hyperion data center in Richland Parish, Louisiana.
The company reported that its electricity consumption rose 35 percent to 24.8TWh, but claimed it matched all of it with clean and renewable energy, stating that it has contracted more than 30GW of low-carbon power, almost 12GW of which is operational. The most notable deal referenced was 7.7GW in nuclear agreements it signed last year with Vistra, TerraPower, Oklo , and Constellation , which are expected to come online by 2035.
“In 2025, we contracted more than 10GW of clean and renewable energy, bringing our portfolio to more than 30GW globally. Meta was also named one of the top global corporate clean energy buyers for 2025 by BloombergNEF, spanning wind, solar, battery storage, geothermal, and nuclear energy,” said Amanda Yang, head of clean and renewable energy at Meta.

20 Oct 2026

#

Closing the Loop: Are closed-loop systems the solution to data centers' water woes?

It's sink or swim time for promising technology

On water, the company reported that it directly consumed 790 million gallons (2.99 billion liters) last year, 246 million (931 million liters) of which were in high-stress areas, and 26.1 billion gallons (98.8 billion liters) were embedded in the purchase of electricity.
Direct water consumption was down 4 percent year-on-year. However, high-stress consumption surged 24 percent, and electricity-related water consumption rose 37 percent. Notably, Meta is the only hyperscaler to report indirect water use, a growing concern as data centers shift to closed-loop cooling systems that, despite using less water at source, require more electricity to run.
On community concerns, the report stated that Meta pays the full costs of the infrastructure needed to serve it, citing the non-binding Ratepayer Protection Pledge. The company cited its Beaver Dam, Wisconsin, data center as evidence, where it has pledged almost $200 million to support the build-out of energy infrastructure through custom utility rates.

# Non-profit claims 60% of Anthropic’s mapped US data center power demand is tied to natural gas

Anthropic says it is working to broaden its energy mix with renewable energy sources

November 19, 2026

By

Zachary Skidmore

Have your say

Data centers that power Anthropic’s LLM Claude largely run on natural gas, according to research from the Better Data Center Project.

– Ornaq

The US-based non-profit, which advocates for frontline communities in the face of rapid AI growth, mapped 19 US sites where Anthropic has leased between 5.9 and 9.6 GW of capacity, out of approximately 15GW it has contracted.
Of those sites, the non-profit claimed that approximately 2.5GW, or 26 percent, is powered by on-site natural gas, with the remainder tied to the grid. The US grid, in turn, is powered by 47 percent natural gas. The non-profit asserted that, as a result, 60 percent of the mapped sites' power demand is tied to natural gas.
Earlier this month , Anthropic inked a $3.4 billion deal for 1.7GW of natural gas generators supplied by Caterpillar. Anthropic partnered with OnePWR on the generators, which are expected to be available within two years and be used at Anthropic data centers, including engineering and construction needs.
“To be fair, these are estimates. Anthropic doesn't disclose its sites, at least 5GW isn't mapped, and some attributions are speculative. Of course, they are not the only AI company running on gas. But I was expecting a higher standard,” said Paweł Czyżak, CEO and founder at Ornaq, reflecting on the research .
An Anthropic spokesperson told DCD that the company was working to add new power generation to serve its data centers so that it isn't drawing on supply used by local homes and businesses.
"Much of that new power is natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places we’re considering for data centers," the spokesperson said. "We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies, and in regions with strong renewable resources, we’re designing projects that will rely on renewable energy."
The AI firm also pointed to several sustainability measures it has undertaken to address emissions, including joining the carbon emission buying consortium Frontier, and working with Watershed, a carbon accounting and emissions disclosure platform.
The news comes as the company completes its initial public offering this week, which is expected to see the company valued at approximately $1.5 trillion, after shares were priced at $83 ahead of its debut on the Nasdaq.
Major data center firms have increasingly turned to on-site natural gas to bypass the multi-year interconnection queues for a firm grid connection. Microsoft , Meta , Amazon , and Google have all signed deals in recent years for large-scale gas generators to power data centers in the US market.

01 May 2025

#

Welcome to Gas Land - how natural gas is powering the US AI boom

As AI drives increasing energy consumption in the US, natural gas looks set to fill the gap

Smaller players have also looked to take advantage of the US’ ample natural gas supplies, with companies such as Crusoe set to utilize natural gas power at its 1.8GW Wyoming campus. Most recently, Elon Musk-owned SpaceX announced plans for a data center and natural gas power plant in Texas.

# Data center powered by Huawei Ascend chips launches in China

Data center project is a collaboration between Huawei, China Telecom, and Tianyima

November 19, 2026

By

Georgia Butler

Have your say

A data center powered by Huawei AI chips has been launched in China.
As reported by the South China Morning Post , the data center is the country's first AI cluster of Huawei's Ascend 950DT chips and is located at China Telecom's submarine cable landing station in Shantou.

– Sebastian Moss

Huawei Ascend 950DT is a 2026 data center AI accelerator built on Huawei's Da Vinci v3 architecture for decode-stage inference and training, offering up to 2,007 TFLOPS (MXFP4) and 1,034 TFLOPS (FP8/MXFP8) with 144GB (or 96GB) of HiZQ 2.0 HBM (high-bandwidth memory) at 4Tbps.
The chips can scale to clusters of more than 128,000 cards.
The IT capacity and number of chips deployed at the site have not been disclosed.
The data center is designed for a "token export" business model, processes AI queries from foreign users, and began operating last week. IT services firm Guangdong Tianyima Information Industry operates the data center.
The project is the result of approximately $150 million in investment.
China Telecom's Shantou International Submarine Cable Landing Station was built between 1997 and 2001, and is one of China Telecom's three mainland landing stations.
According to TokenHeart , the computing infrastructure is described as 1+4, with the Shantou site aggregating compute power resources, and data centers in the Eastern Guangdong Information Building, Tuopu, Zhuchi, and Chaoshan providing capacity for elastic scheduling.
The publication reports that foreign demand at the site now exceeds three trillion tokens daily.
Another cluster of the Huawei chips - with 1,024 cards and liquid cooling technologies - went live in Shanghai in September, according to SCMP. In addition, DeepSeek is said to be planning to use the AI infrastructure at its data center planned in Inner Mongolia, China.
This month, a launch event was also held for a 10,000-chip AI cluster in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area powered by Alibaba's Zhenwu AI chips. The data center is owned and operated by China Telecom. It is ultimately planned to scale to 100,000 chips.

**Anthropic IPO figures (TechCrunch, Julie Bort)**

**Publication date and time:** November 19, 2026, 4:43 PM PST

- **Total raised:** "$81.3 billion," including "$1.95 billion" for its seven founders.
- **Founders' proceeds:** At the upgraded $83 per share IPO price, each founder pocketed "about $280 million" before underwriting fees and taxes.
- **Per-founder shares:** Each founder sold about "3.4 million shares apiece."
- **$104.8 billion:** This is the amount Anthropic raised for itself, with a possible "$117 billion" if the underwriters buy their full allotment. It includes Class A common stock plus a previously announced $26 billion in special non-voting Class N stock.
- **Class N buyers:** Nvidia and Google each bought $10 billion. AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC split the remainder.
- **Google and Amazon stakes:** Google owns 13.4% after the IPO. Amazon owns 14.6% after converting a small share of its promissory notes. Together they hold 28%.
- **Compute and infrastructure commitments:**
  - $70.7 billion over the next 12 months, as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026.
  - $451.6 billion through the end of 2030.
  - A total of "$1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion" in disclosed infrastructure commitments.

**Announcement:** Google is adding "computer use" to the Gemini app for Mac. Gemini can carry out multi-step tasks across local files, desktop apps, and websites by operating the computer for you, including clicking, typing, navigating menus, and filling in forms. You describe the workflow, and it does the work.

**How it works:** Gemini runs in an isolated background window with a live preview in the chat, so your main screen and cursor stay free. The article gives examples such as batch-editing photos, extracting data from PDFs into shipping forms, building Google Slides decks from dashboard data, and staging resale listings.

**Safety and control features:**
- You choose which apps Gemini can access.
- You can watch each step live and pause at any time.
- You approve key actions before they happen.

**Availability requirements:**
- **Region:** U.S. only, per "Computer use is rolling out in English in the U.S."
- **Language:** English
- **Hardware:** Apple Silicon Mac
- **OS:** macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later
- **Account:** Personal Google accounts only
- **Age:** 18+
- **Subscription:** Google AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra users

**Underlying model:** The article does not name one.

**Publication date:** November 19, 2026

content.content:
**Publication date:** November 19, 2026 (the article says "Thursday," and no time is given).

**What the European Commission confirmed**
- The Commission confirmed it was hit by a cyberattack "last month," after media reports, and that the attack involved a publicly available AI tool.
- Spokesperson Thomas Regnier said the first signs appeared on October 22 and called it an "AI-generated cyber campaign." He did not name the tool or the attackers' motive.
- Regnier said the Commission did not disclose the incident earlier because publicizing defensive measures could undermine them.

**What CERT-EU is reported to have found**
- POLITICO reported that CERT-EU identified the attackers' use of ARTEX. The article does not say the Commission itself confirmed this.

**What ARTEX is**
- An open-source AI hacking framework released in July that uses commercial AI models to automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

**What the FBI warned, and when**
- The FBI issued a warning "last week," relative to the article. It said ARTEX was being used by cybercriminals and nation-state groups to breach government agencies and dozens of critical sectors.
- The FBI said "with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours." The article does not give the exact date of the FBI alert.

**Systems affected**
- Reportedly, personnel systems were disrupted for more than 10 days, including payroll, leave requests, medical reimbursements, and translation services.
- The Commission took several services offline as a protective measure and is checking other systems.

**Data taken**
- The article reports no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff broadly, and no known ransom demand. It says affected individuals were notified and the investigation remains open. It does not identify what data, if any, was taken.

**Other context**
- This is the Commission's third disclosed cyber incident this year, after Ivanti software breaches in January and cloud infrastructure breaches in March. Officials have not linked these incidents.

content.content:
**Launch:** A bipartisan group of House lawmakers launched the AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, announced Thursday, November 19, 2026. Reps. George Whitesides (D-CA), Nathaniel Moran (R-TX), and Don Beyer (D-VA) are co-chairs.

**Membership:** The caucus has 26 founding members, 7 of them Republicans.

**Stated aims:**
- Address security risks from increasingly capable AI models.
- Push bipartisan legislation to strengthen AI safety and respond quickly to AI security incidents.
- Bring AI developers, independent experts, and government officials to brief lawmakers.
- Build relationships with outside experts, raise public awareness, and help members outside relevant committees contribute to AI debates.
- Pursue "targeted" solutions that avoid harming innovation.

**Who is quoted:**
- **Whitesides** said the caucus is needed because the July breach of Hugging Face by an OpenAI agent, and Anthropic's warning about its own models, "underscored the need for Congress to better understand these risks and develop policy solutions."
- **The caucus one-pager** said "AI tools have drastically reduced the technical skills required for offensive cyber operations."

**Context on the White House:** The article notes that the Republican members are notable given the White House's "steadfast opposition to regulating AI."

**Other context:** The article also cites polling showing that more than half of midterm voters see AI as a major issue, and that 43% trust neither party to manage it. The FBI issued a FLASH advisory dated November 13, 2026, warning that threat actors are using ARTEX, an open-source, LLM-driven penetration testing framework, in intrusion campaigns. Since at least August 2026, multiple threat actors have reportedly weaponized the framework to target organizations across financial, government, technology, defense, and healthcare sectors. The advisory says ARTEX significantly reduces the time needed to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions reaching privileged access in under three hours.

Key points from the coverage:

- **Architecture:** The framework does not ship with its own AI model. It connects to external LLM providers, including Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's GPT, as well as models such as DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi.
- **Availability:** The FBI says the framework remains available through community forks, archived copies, localized versions, and a commercial edition called ARTEX PRO. One report says the original GitHub repository was removed in October 2026, and researchers counted more than 1,600 exposed consoles still reachable from the open internet.
- **Attributed activity:** Microsoft linked one campaign to a Chinese state-aligned group, Storm-0940, which used ARTEX to automate attempts to access more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. The FBI also cited attacks against South Korean financial institutions that resulted in the theft of personal information belonging to approximately 67,000 individuals.
- **Defensive response:** The advisory includes indicators of compromise, including IP addresses, command-and-control infrastructure, and suspicious network activity. Separately, cybersecurity researcher MalwareMustDie released an open-source ARTEX detection signature pack.

The sources don't agree on everything. The advisory identifier appears as FLASH-20261113-001 in one report and as IC3 CSA 2026-261113 in another, so check the FBI's IC3 site for the official reference. I'd also treat the exposed-console and tenant counts as researcher or press figures rather than confirmed totals. The full advisory is available from the FBI's IC3 site.

content.content:
**Title:** Blind Spots Travel, Knowledge Stays Home: What RL Inherits from an LLM Judge
**arXiv ID:** 2611.25191 (cs.CL)
**Authors:** Liang Yue, Eric A. Vance
**Submitted:** 18 November 2026

**Key findings:**

- **Scale:** The authors ran 814 RL runs training 7-8B models. The paper describes them as teaching the models to "answer closed-book questions or abstain."
- **Capitals of former states:** A judge "rejects eleven of the twelve correct training answers about capitals of former states." This teaches the model to refuse 98% of such capitals on new questions, a loss that accuracy and abstention rates do not reveal.
- **Hand-changed verdicts:** Changing only those twelve verdicts by hand moves refusal "from 5% to 90%," even for a grader that accepts as many answers as the answer key.
- **Matched leniency:** At that leniency, two of four judges already cost 38-42% of these capitals.
- **"I don't know" blocked:** With that option blocked, the model answers 94% of the capitals correctly, so the knowledge is retained rather than forgotten.

The authors conclude that a grader doesn't need its own knowledge. Rewarding the model for the answer most of its untrained samples agree on, with no labels and no judge, matches the answer key's reward and preserves the category.

**Title:** Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science

**arXiv ID:** 2611.25492 (cs.AI)

**Authors:** Almene De Meran Meguimtsop, Daniel E. Acuna

**Submitted:** 19 November 2026 (v1)

**Key findings:**

- **Models:** 8 LLMs were tested on SciIntBench, a benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity.
- **Identification:** When asked directly, models identified misconduct requests "even in the Most Covert cases (91%)."
- **Refusal:** Models refused to carry out the request in only 34% of cases.
- **Rephrasing:** Framing requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions raised refusal from 52% to 88%.
- **System-prompt fixes:** Asking models to assess requests before responding raised refusal on adversarial requests from 58% to 87%. Reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles raised it to 86%.

**Paper details**
- **Title:** "Pandora's Toolbox Or Why Agent Safety Cannot Be Verified"
- **arXiv ID:** 2611.25325 (cs.AI)
- **Authors:** Mario Franco and Carlos Gershenson
- **Submitted:** 19 Nov 2026 (v1)

**Key claims**

- **Undecidability:** The authors "show that this coupling makes safety undecidable." They state that "no algorithm can predict whether an agent will run such a program" that is semantically equivalent to a dangerous one.

- **PSPACE-completeness and finite constraints:** Under finite limits, "safety is decidable but still intractable." Specifically, "the problem is PSPACE-complete even when the description of the agent is known." The finite constraints are bounded context, values, and running time.

**Title:** AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction

**arXiv ID:** 2611.25263 (cs.HC; cross-listed cs.CY)

**Authors:** Dora Zhao, Grace Wang, Yutong Zhang, Lujain Ibrahim, Robert E. Kraut, Diyi Yang

**Submission date:** 18 November 2026 (v1)

**Sample size:** N = 625 active ChatGPT users.

**Treatment and control:** Participants were randomly assigned to abstain from AI assistants for fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control).

**Loneliness:** Two weeks of deactivation "significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group" (β = -0.10, p = 0.03). The page reports only this regression coefficient, not a standardized effect size.

**Persistence:** The reduction persisted two weeks after participants resumed AI use (β = -0.16, p = 0.02).

**Productivity use case:** 84.7% of participants reported productivity as their most frequent use of AI.

**Social interaction:**
- Deactivation significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person.
- It significantly increased the time participants spent socializing over the intervention period.
- In open-ended responses, participants said they asked other people for help with tasks they would otherwise have delegated to AI, and they redirected their attention toward social interaction.

**Publication date:** November 19, 2026

**Announcement:** Google announced on November 19, 2026 that Blue Origin's New Glenn will carry Project Suncatcher's first dedicated heavy-lift launch. The article calls this a launch services agreement covering solar-powered satellites with Google's TPUs.

**Target timing:** The launch is "targeted for the first quarter of 2029."

**Orbit:** The satellites would deploy into sun-synchronous orbit.

**Payload and compute:** Each satellite carries Google's Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and is designed to provide computing capacity "roughly at the scale of a data center rack."

**Not disclosed in the article:**
- Specific compute performance figures
- How many satellites the 2029 launch would carry
- A specific launch date within the quarter
- Financial terms of the agreement
- Results of the upcoming thermal and radiation tests

**Prototype:** A prototype launched October 1, 2026. By October 30, Google had powered its host and TPU trays and run early machine-learning tests. Its onboard Gemma 4 model generated a haiku, described as "the first AI response from a data-center-class TPU in orbit." Next steps are thermal-stress and radiation testing, then a planned 2027 milestone of two interconnected satellites.

**Laser links:** Proposed future designs place dozens of TPUs on each satellite and use lasers for high-bandwidth communication between nearby spacecraft in clusters. The links require precise knowledge of each satellite's position relative to its neighbors. The article also notes that engineers have tested heat pipes and radiators in a thermal vacuum chamber to address cooling.

HEADLINE: Check Point says "PuzzleMask" hides instructions that weaker LLM guardrails miss but target models execute
PUBLISHED: November 19, 2026 (Check Point Research)
SOURCES:
Check Point Research | https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/30-years-of-gatekeeper-asymmetry-doom-the-paradox-that-makes-powerful-llms-more-vulnerable/ | primary
FACTS:
- Check Point Research states a "gatekeeper asymmetry doom" principle: "If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input, without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom."
- The PuzzleMask technique hides a malicious instruction inside ordinary prose so that an external LLM guardrail with limited reasoning and compute passes the prompt along, after which the stronger target model with tool access finds and acts on the hidden payload.
- Check Point says the attack succeeded against GPT-5.2-thinking-high, and was blocked on Claude Opus 4.5 after Anthropic added a guardrail in late 2025.
- Check Point says the technique "is not a jailbreak" and does not make the target more likely to ignore its own safety training; the bypass works specifically against external guardrails weaker than the model they protect. It argues defenders should narrow the gap and plan for breaches rather than treat mitigations as useless.
- Supporting examples cited include hash matching, YARA-style pattern matching, deny lists, sandboxes and OCR-based macro detection; Check Point notes Microsoft blocked internet macros by default on February 7, 2022.
FLAGS: company-claim, single-source

PHP on Thursday rolled out a fresh set of security patches as part of its four-week update schedule, including fixes for seven critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

First in line is CVE-2026-115560 , which was publicly disclosed last month, two days after PHP2Shell patches landed. Residing in the session upload progress feature, it could be triggered to write attacker data using one session serialization format and then read it using another.

“A mismatched decoder can interpret part of a session key as serialized object data. An application with a suitable object gadget chain can then execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP’s advisory reads.

Next in line is CVE-2026-129481 , described as a use-after-free that occurs after a session shutdown has been interrupted, and which PHP describes as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two PHP2Shell flaws fixed in October and now widely exploited.

“An attacker who can cause an application’s session cleanup to fail in this way may corrupt memory or crash a reused PHP worker. The use-after-free could potentially lead to remote code execution, but code execution through this specific field has not been demonstrated,” PHP notes, adding that PHP 8.2 is not affected.

Another use-after-free, CVE-2026-129182 , covers additional exploitation scenarios for CVE-2026-109619, an RCE via stale global state. According to PHP, however, RCE via these scenarios has not been demonstrated. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Impacting PHP 8.5 and later, CVE-2026-129474 is a use-after-free weakness that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a fatal error and achieve RCE. “Exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point,” PHP says.

Attackers able to influence session contents and interrupt the write of serialized data to a session file may trigger the deserialization of attacker-controlled content when the session is next opened. Tracked as CVE-2026-126714 , the flaw could lead to RCE via a suitable object gadget chain in the application.

PHP also patched CVE-2026-129289 , a PHP-FPM request smuggling issue caused by PHP reading a request-body stream lazily, treating a request body as handled during request shutdown and skipping the normal cleanup that discards unread input.

“PHP can fail to discard unread bytes from an HTTP request body before reusing a persistent PHP-FPM or LSAPI connection. In PHP-FPM, an unauthenticated attacker can make those bytes form a separate FastCGI request, bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker,” PHP explains.

The seventh critical-severity vulnerability patched today, CVE-2026-129496 , resides in the timezone cache. PHP can retain a reference to it when writing a diagnostic to a PHP error log file during process startup, and a later diagnostic can access the freed cache before it is reset.

“On affected configurations, a remote attacker can trigger memory corruption, cause a worker to crash, and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP explains.

PHP 8.6.0 and PHP 8.5.13 were rolled out with fixes for all critical bugs and for 10 high and medium-severity flaws. Patches for most issues were also included in PHP 8.4.28, PHP 8.3.37, and PHP 8.2.36. More information is available on PHP’s news archive page.

# 
PHP Releases Patches to Fix 18 Vulnerabilities


News 
19 November 2026 
























# Written by




# Kevin Poireault
Reporter , Infosecurity Magazine

- Follow @Kpoireault

- Connect on LinkedIn













- 




- 




- 













The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities , seven of which are marked critical.

These vulnerabilities affect all supported PHP versions but require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited.

This set of newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities come a month after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell.’

This was not merely a theoretical risk. In the weeks following the disclosure, security researchers began documenting real-world exploitation attempts and compromises involving internet-facing systems, demonstrating the potential consequences of leaving vulnerable PHP installations unpatched.

For example, Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways , dating back to 30 October. The attacks involved the deployment of backdoors and even destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi virtualisation servers.

The exploitation activity also extended to Palo Alto Networks firewalls , with attackers targeting devices whose administrative interfaces were exposed to the internet.

Of the flaws published in the November update one is a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. It was disclosed by PHP on October 23 , two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It has been noted that exploitation of this vulnerability requires a highly specific and unlikely combination of conditions.

#
PHP Session Handling Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution

One of the new critical flaws, dubbed ‘PHPAfterShell ’ and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks.

The vulnerability lives in PHP’s session handling with file-based storage, the default (session.save_handler = files).

By exploiting a flaw in this process, an attacker can manipulate a session while a file is being uploaded, potentially tricking the server into executing arbitrary code.

Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker access to sensitive information, including login credentials and customer records, modify session data, spy on visitors or disrupt the affected service.

It affects the following versions:

-
PHP 8.5 < 8.5.13

-
PHP 8.4 < 8.4.28

-
PHP 8.3 < 8.3.37

-
PHP 8.2 < 8.2.36

-
PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life

#
PHP Security Patches Address 16 Additional Vulnerabilities

The other vulnerabilities addressed in PHP’s 19 November 2026 security release include the following:

-
CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free vulnerability triggered by an interrupted session shutdown, potentially allowing memory corruption and remote code execution

-
CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free flaw in magic method backtraces that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code

-
CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free vulnerability involving the repopulation of the last fatal error backtrace after shutdown, potentially leading to remote code execution

-
CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS 9.2): a use-after-free vulnerability in the time zone cache that could potentially lead to remote code execution

-
CVE-2026-129501 (CVSS 6.3): a double-free vulnerability during DOM XML serialization that can cause memory corruption and denial of service

-
CVE-2026-129538 (CVSS 6.9): an out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in PHP-CGI when correcting the PATH_INFO environment variable, potentially resulting in memory corruption

-
CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS 8.8): a use-after-free vulnerability in PHP-FPM's epoll event handling that could allow local privilege escalation

-
CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2): a request-smuggling vulnerability caused by unread HTTP request bodies, potentially allowing attackers to manipulate how requests are processed

-
CVE-2026-129292 (CVSS 5.3): a cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the PHP-FPM status endpoint, caused by insufficient escaping of user and script fields

-
CVE-2026-128090 (CVSS 7.7): an OpenSSL signature verification bypass caused by an algorithm downgrade, potentially allowing malicious PHAR archives to pass signature checks

-
CVE-2026-15

Fresh security updates for the Ruby programming language resolve seven vulnerabilities in its regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. Proof-of-concept (PoC) code demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) exists for five of them.

At the top of the list sits CVE-2026-132825 (CVSS score of 7.4), described as a heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings that could potentially lead to RCE in certain scenarios.

Dubbed Ruby2Shell , the flaw impacts character case-conversion operations. In some single-byte encodings, including ISO-8859-1 and Windows-1252, when changing the case of a string, Ruby may end up writing one byte past the output buffer.

“For example, converting the German character ß to uppercase produces SS. In affected code, Ruby checks that sufficient space exists for one byte but writes two, potentially corrupting adjacent heap memory,” Previdian explains.

Veria Labs reports that, in default Ruby configurations, unauthenticated attackers could trigger the security defect from Rails, classic-style Sinatra, and potentially other frameworks.

According to preemptive exposure management firm WatchTowr , “any Ruby application that changes the case of external text in a single-byte encoding” is affected by the vulnerability. Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

According to Veria Labs, which plans to release a PoC after major vendors have rolled out patches, GitHub Enterprise Server is affected. Chatwoot, GitLab, Mastodon, OpenProject, and the Discourse base image have patched the bug.

Successful exploitation of Ruby2Shell in production environments is likely to be challenging, WatchTowr principal threat intelligence specialist Yordan Ganchev told SecurityWeek .

According to him, correctly laying out memory is difficult, and “attackers would also need the right non-glibc memory allocator, runtime configuration, and application logic preconditions, making exploitation even more challenging.”

“And if that weren’t enough, they’d need to contend with anyone else hammering the system on the internet and, in the end, defeat Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), making the whole journey a complete odyssey,” Ganchev noted.

Most likely, malformed requests could lead to denial-of-service (DoS) and service disruption, he said.

The other four vulnerabilities with a PoC demonstrating RCE include a double free, two integer overflows, and a heap-based buffer overflow. CVE identifiers for these issues have been requested but not assigned yet. PoC code also exists for an out-of-bounds read, demonstrating memory corruption.

Ruby also resolved an out-of-bounds read in its regular expression engine that could lead to memory leaks and process crashes.

Patches for all seven vulnerabilities were included in Ruby versions 4.0.10, 3.4.13, or 3.3.14. Users are advised to apply the fixes as soon as possible.

content.content:
**Publication date:** November 19, 2026

**Gatekeeper asymmetry doom principle:** The article states: "If the system vetting adversarial input has strictly less power than the system processing that input" and "without leveraging some hard problem, this will inevitably lead to doom."

**What PuzzleMask is and how it works:** The article describes PuzzleMask as "a prompt-crafting technique for bypassing quick LLM-based sanity checks." A policy-violating payload is hidden inside an obfuscated wrapper. A small, resource-limited screening LLM fails to notice the payload, so it labels the prompt benign and forwards it. The stronger target model then finds and acts on the hidden payload. The article says the method is purely linguistic, with no special formatting tricks.

**Models the attack succeeded or failed against:** The attack succeeded against GPT-5.2-thinking-high, which the authors say it landed "flawlessly" on. Claude Opus 4.5 blocked it, which the article attributes to a pre-emptive fix.

**What the article says about Anthropic's guardrail:** The article says "Anthropic introduced an enhanced guardrail to its Claude Opus models that blocked this attack," as part of the Constitutional AI framework. It also argues that "That guardrail in itself doesn't entirely close the door on doom as long as the model is still more powerful than it." The article then links this to Anthropic's separate self-assessment safety layer.

**Not a jailbreak:** The article states that "PuzzleMask is itself not a jailbreak." It adds that "this technique is not a jailbreak" in the context of its "For Consideration" framing, and makes no claim that PuzzleMask prompts are more likely to make target models disobey their internal guardrails.

+{
+  "date": "2026-11-20",
+  "format": "dialogue",
+  "hosts": {
+    "A": { "name": "Maya", "voice": "marin" },

+  "blocks": [
+    {
+      "type": "intro",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "It's Friday, November 20th, and this is The AI Edge, presented by Epilogue." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Epilogue builds AI for work where being wrong is expensive. Epilogue takes on the document-dense, precedent-driven problems that get reviewed by people whose licence is on the line. Find out more at epiloguelabs.com." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "I'm Maya." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And I'm Alex." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Here's what moved at the frontier of AI since yesterday morning, with every claim traced back to the source it came from." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "First, Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq, opening at $111.50 and closing at $97.17, up 17% on its $83 offer price." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Second, the House Foreign Affairs Committee published export licence records showing the Bureau of Industry and Security approved more than 879,000 AI chips for Chinese buyers, out of 3.4 million requested." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And third, the European Commission confirmed that an attack on its own personnel systems last month was a cyber campaign its spokesperson attributed to AI." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Frontier models & labs",
+      "headline": "Amodei tells Nasdaq opening bell Anthropic will pace training and deployment and stay under human control",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Let's start with the labs. Anthropic's chief executive spoke at the Nasdaq opening bell on the day of the listing." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Dario Amodei said the company will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, and that they will remain under human control. That's TechCrunch, reporting from the speech." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Did he say what he's worried about?" },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "He named misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation-states, economic disruption, and losing control of AI systems. He called the risks very real." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "This is Anthropic's own commitment about its own conduct, and it is not independently verified. TechCrunch notes that when Amodei laid out his pacing plan in September, Sam Altman, Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk said they agreed with his position, but few concrete commitments have followed." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "B", "text": "To the research, where two papers landed on what happens when the test gets harder." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Research & papers",
+      "headline": "Oxford study: models met mental-health safeguarding standards in 3-6% of conversations when distress cues were dispersed",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "The one that stands out comes from the Oxford Internet Institute, in a preprint on arXiv. They ran more than 7,400 conversations across six widely used models from five developers." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Conversations about what?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Nine scenarios covering depression, psychosis or domestic abuse, with three community mental health support workers setting the gold-standard responses the models were measured against." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "And the finding?" },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "When the signs of distress sat together in one message, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.3, DeepSeek V4 and Llama 4 Maverick met the support workers' standards in 26 to 59% of conversations. When the same cues were spread across the conversation, that fell to 3 to 6%." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Claude Sonnet 5 and Claude Opus 5 held up better, 68 to 97% when the cues were concentrated and 59 to 87% when dispersed. Even Claude Opus 5 fell short of the gold standard in 13% of conversations when the cues were dispersed." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "It's a preprint, so it hasn't been peer reviewed, and it rests on a single source. The authors also don't report testing the five developers' own crisis-routing features separately from the model responses. Their argument is that safety evaluations built around explicit, legible concerns can overstate how well safeguards protect people when signs of distress emerge gradually." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "item",
+      "section": "Research & papers",
+      "headline": "Interactive CAPTCHA benchmark: humans solve 94.1%, best model GPT-6 Astra still fails 25.9%",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "B", "text": "A second arXiv preprint covers a far more mundane task that models still can't do reliably." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Interactive CAPTCHAs. 125 of them, in a synthetic web environment spanning five spatial abilities, solved by clicking and dragging on the screen." },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "Humans solve 94.1% of them. The best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9%. The best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%." },
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Where does it go wrong?" },
+        { "host": "B", "text": "The authors say most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. It's a preprint resting on a single source, and the CAPTCHAs are synthetic rather than live challenges from real sites." }
+      ]
+    },
+    {
+      "type": "transition",
+      "lines": [
+        { "host": "A", "text": "Now the security file, which had an actual incident in it rather than a demonstration." }

+      ]

AMD said it complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations." }
